Rep. Green’s rural healthcare bills are a rare D.C. win—finally tackling the crisis of shuttered hospitals. The Save America’s Rural Hospitals Act (H.R. 833) cuts Medicare sequestration (Section 101) and removes CRNA supervision (Section 202), freeing rural clinics from bureaucratic chokeholds. But let’s be real: this fixes what D.C. broke. Taxpayers shouldn’t fund endless Medicare fraud while rural ERs close. Real reform means slashing red tape, not just patching it.

Medicaid expansion for CRNA services (Section 203) is a step toward sanity—rural areas need care, not more NIH-funded studies. Why does it take Congress decades to act? Because bureaucrats profit from chaos.

This isn’t “reform”—it’s basic accountability. If D.C. cared, they’d have fixed this years ago. Now they’re scrambling to save face while rural America still waits.

Taxpayers deserve better than Band-Aid fixes. Cut the waste, secure rural care, and stop letting bureaucrats loot the system.

The Rural ER Access Act (H.R. 1129) cuts through bureaucratic red tape by removing Medicare’s 35-mile radius requirement for off-campus emergency facilities. This bill directly addresses how outdated regulations strangle rural healthcare access, forcing hospitals to close due to arbitrary distance rules. 

By eliminating this restriction, it empowers rural emergency departments to operate freely, ensuring 24/7 care for underserved communities without D.C.’s suffocating oversight. ACEP’s endorsement proves this isn’t just policy—it’s a lifeline for patients in crisis. 

Time to let rural hospitals breathe, not suffocate under federal micromanagement.

Prior authorization is a perfect example of bureaucratic bloat that puts paperwork over patients. The Doctor Knows Best Act (H.R.639) nails the problem—government-mandated delays in care cost lives while insurers and bureaucrats pocket profits. $175 billion in annual overpayments prove the system’s broken when bean-counters override doctors. 

Rep. Green’s bill aligns with the core mission: slash red tape that lets D.C. middlemen profit from suffering. Every minute spent justifying necessary treatment to clerks is a minute stolen from patient care. The solution isn’t more oversight—it’s letting medical professionals practice medicine without drowning in compliance theater. 

When insurers dictate care through prior auth, it’s not cost control—it’s rationing by spreadsheet. Time to put patients before paperwork.

Prior authorization is a symptom of a broken system where bureaucrats override doctors, wasting time and taxpayer money. The Doctor Knows Best Act (H.R. 639) tackles this head-on by eliminating red tape that delays critical care. Medicare’s $31.10B in improper payments and Medicaid’s $1.8B fraud settlements prove the current model prioritizes paperwork over patients. 

When insurers deny 24% of claims over $250K and 35% of providers upcode bills, it’s clear the real issue isn’t oversight—it’s a profit-driven bureaucracy. This bill aligns with exposing systemic waste: $10.3M wasted on self-auditing contracts and $4.7B in terminated wasteful agreements show why doctors, not administrators, should steer care. 

Cutting prior authorization isn’t just about speed—it’s about dismantling a rigged system that enriches middlemen while Americans suffer.
